## Bobby Jindal Chosen to Deliver Republican Response to Obama Address

**WASHINGTON** — Louisiana Gov. Bobby Jindal, a rising figure in the Republican Party and one of its most prominent young elected officials, has been selected to deliver the GOP response to President Barack Obama’s address to a joint session of Congress, Republican leaders announced.

Jindal’s selection places the 37-year-old governor at the center of the national political stage at a moment when Republicans are searching for a new voice after losing the White House and suffering major congressional setbacks in the 2008 elections. Obama’s speech, expected to focus heavily on the economy, the financial crisis and the newly enacted stimulus package, will be followed by Jindal’s televised remarks outlining the Republican alternative.

The Louisiana governor has been widely viewed within GOP circles as one of the party’s most promising national figures. He is young, policy-oriented, socially conservative and has a personal story that Republicans believe can broaden the party’s appeal. His appearance will give him one of the most visible speaking opportunities in American politics: the opposition party’s official response to a president’s major address.

### A rising Republican figure

Jindal, the son of immigrants from India, was born in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. His parents moved to the United States before he was born, and his biography has long been central to his political identity. He has often described his family’s story as evidence of American opportunity and has emphasized education, hard work and public service throughout his career.

A graduate of Brown University, Jindal studied biology and public policy and later attended Oxford University as a Rhodes Scholar. He converted to Catholicism as a young adult and has become a favorite of many social conservatives for his positions on abortion, religious liberty and family issues.

Jindal entered public service at an unusually young age. In his 20s, he was appointed secretary of the Louisiana Department of Health and Hospitals, where he was credited by supporters with helping address budget problems in the state’s health care system. He later served in Washington in the Department of Health and Human Services during President George W. Bush’s administration.

In 2004, Jindal won election to the U.S. House of Representatives from Louisiana’s 1st Congressional District. Three years later, he was elected governor of Louisiana, becoming the first Indian-American governor in U.S. history and one of the youngest governors in the country.

### Katrina recovery and Louisiana leadership

Jindal’s governorship has been shaped in part by the long recovery from Hurricane Katrina, the 2005 storm that devastated New Orleans and much of the Gulf Coast. Although Katrina struck before Jindal became governor, the recovery effort was still a central issue when he took office in 2008.

As governor, Jindal inherited a state still struggling with rebuilding homes, restoring infrastructure, repairing schools and hospitals, and managing federal recovery funds. He pushed to speed up recovery programs, improve state management and strengthen Louisiana’s ability to respond to future disasters.

His first year in office was also marked by another major test: hurricanes Gustav and Ike in 2008. Jindal received praise from many Republicans and some emergency management observers for his highly visible role during Gustav, when he coordinated evacuations, briefed the public frequently and remained in Louisiana rather than traveling to the Republican National Convention. His handling of those storms helped elevate his national profile and reinforced his image as a hands-on executive.

Jindal has often contrasted Louisiana’s improved storm response after Katrina with the failures that surrounded the 2005 disaster, arguing that competence and accountability in government are essential. Republicans are likely to highlight that record as part of his appeal in responding to Obama’s agenda.

### Role in the McCain campaign

During the 2008 presidential campaign, Jindal was a prominent supporter and surrogate for Republican nominee Sen. John McCain. He was frequently mentioned as a possible vice-presidential contender, though McCain ultimately selected Alaska Gov. Sarah Palin as his running mate.

Jindal campaigned for the Republican ticket and appeared at party events, but his role during the Republican National Convention was affected by Hurricane Gustav. As the storm approached the Gulf Coast, Jindal stayed in Louisiana to oversee preparations and emergency response rather than delivering a major convention speech in St. Paul, Minnesota. That decision drew attention and helped bolster his reputation as a governor focused on his state during a crisis.

His selection to deliver the Republican response now gives him a national platform he did not fully receive during the convention.

### Republican message after stimulus fight

Obama’s address comes shortly after Congress passed a massive economic stimulus package aimed at combating the recession. Republicans overwhelmingly opposed the legislation, arguing that it included too much spending, too little tax relief and insufficient measures to spur long-term job creation.

Jindal is expected to focus on limited government, fiscal restraint and conservative economic principles. He has criticized federal spending increases and positioned himself as a reform-minded governor. His response will likely aim to draw a sharp contrast with Obama’s approach while presenting Republicans as supportive of recovery but opposed to what they view as excessive government expansion.

The assignment is politically significant but risky. The opposition response is one of the most difficult speeches in politics: delivered after a president speaks before the grandeur of the House chamber, often to a much smaller camera setting, with no applause and little opportunity for spontaneity. It can elevate a politician — or expose weaknesses on a national stage.

### A tradition of high-profile rebuttals

The response to a president’s State of the Union address, or to a similar address before Congress, has long been used by the opposition party to showcase emerging leaders and potential future national candidates.

Past Democratic responders have included Virginia Sen. Jim Webb, who delivered the response to President George W. Bush in 2007, and Kansas Gov. Kathleen Sebelius, who responded in 2008. Sebelius was later chosen by Obama to serve as secretary of health and human services. Former Virginia Gov. Tim Kaine also delivered the Democratic response in 2006.

Republicans have used the platform in previous years to highlight governors, senators and party leaders, including figures such as former New Jersey Gov. Christine Todd Whitman and others seen at the time as representatives of the party’s future or ideological direction.

For Jindal, the speech offers a chance to introduce himself to Americans who know little about him beyond his résumé. It also allows Republicans to present a younger and more diverse face at a time when the party is debating how to rebuild after Obama’s historic election.

### A possible 2012 contender

Even before being selected for the response, Jindal was frequently discussed as a potential 2012 presidential contender. He has repeatedly downplayed such speculation, saying his focus is on Louisiana. Still, his age, biography, conservative credentials and executive experience have made him a regular part of conversations about the GOP’s future.

His response to Obama will be closely watched by Republican activists, donors and strategists looking for leaders who can articulate opposition to the new administration while avoiding the appearance of simply rejecting Obama’s popularity.

The moment is also symbolic. Obama, the nation’s first Black president, will speak from the House chamber after winning office on a message of change and hope. Jindal, the son of Indian immigrants and the first Indian-American governor, will answer for a Republican Party seeking to show that it, too, can represent a changing America.

Whether the speech becomes a launching pad for Jindal or merely a difficult assignment in a challenging political climate will depend on how effectively he can balance criticism of Obama with a positive Republican vision.

For now, GOP leaders are betting that Jindal’s biography, record and conservative message make him the right person to answer the new president at a pivotal moment for both parties.

Obama’s February 24 speech is not technically a State of the Union address — new presidents traditionally wait until their second year to deliver one — but it will carry the same political weight, coming before a joint session of Congress and a national television audience as the administration presses its economic recovery plan.

The opposition response has often served as a high-profile audition for rising political figures. Democrats used the platform in recent years to highlight then-Virginia Gov. Tim Kaine, Sen. Jim Webb and Kansas Gov. Kathleen Sebelius. Republicans have similarly turned to governors and congressional leaders in past rebuttals, using the address to present alternative messages and introduce national audiences to potential future contenders.

By choosing Jindal, Republicans are signaling that they want the GOP response to come from outside the bruising fights on Capitol Hill and from a governor who can speak to fiscal discipline, health care and education reform — issues Jindal has emphasized in Louisiana.

The speech will also place Jindal in a politically delicate position. Obama remains personally popular, and the country is facing a deepening recession, but Republicans are eager to draw sharp contrasts over federal spending, taxes and the size of government.

For Jindal, the rebuttal offers a rare national spotlight. For Republicans, it is a chance to present a younger, more diverse face as they begin rebuilding in the early days of the Obama presidency.
